A GIC ladder is a maturity calendar: match cash releases to spending

Four graphics separate returned principal from interest, compare a five-rung ladder with one five-year term and expose cash needs before maturity.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 3 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Explore a five-rung maturity schedule and annual cash needs

Interactive planning lab

Ladder: total interest paid at maturities$6,329.75
Ladder: additional starting liquid cash needed$0
Single five-year term: additional starting cash needed$43,000

Hypothetical fixed-rate, non-cashable deposits with no default. Capital is invested at time zero. The ladder buys five equal principal amounts with original terms of one to five years; the comparison buys one five-year term. Every term uses the same entered effective annual rate, compounded annually and paid with principal only at maturity. No renewal or reinvestment occurs. Each year’s maturity arrives before that year-end cash need. The separate reserve earns zero. No interim spending, early redemption, automatic rollover, tax, account withdrawal rule, fee, deposit-insurance calculation or rate offer is modeled. Negative cash is an unmet funding need, not automatic borrowing. Returned principal is cash released, not interest income.

The central idea

A maturity can release both capital and interest. The planning question is whether each cash need arrives after enough money becomes accessible.

01

Read the payment and access terms before building a ladder

The FCAC’s GIC disclosure guide identifies contract details that matter: principal repayment, interest payment, early access and automatic reinvestment. A quoted rate alone does not specify when money reaches a spending account.

This illustration buys five equal non-cashable amounts at the start, with original terms of one, two, three, four and five years. Every term uses the same hypothetical 4% effective annual rate, compounded annually. Principal and accumulated interest are paid together at maturity.

Those are selected contract assumptions, not current product offers. An actual ladder can have different rates, interest-payment frequencies, redemption provisions and account restrictions. Confirm the issuer’s agreement and maturity instructions before relying on a release date.

02

Separate interest earned from the capital coming back

CAD 50,000 is split into five CAD 10,000 rungs. The first releases CAD 10,400 after one year: CAD 10,000 of principal and CAD 400 of interest. The second releases CAD 10,816 after two years, including CAD 816 of interest.

The fifth rung releases about CAD 12,166.53 after five years. Across all five original maturities, proceeds total about CAD 56,329.75. Only about CAD 6,329.75 is interest. The remaining CAD 50,000 is the original capital becoming accessible again.

Calling the full maturity stream “income” would overstate the economic gain. The stacked bars keep the two parts visible. Each rung compounds for its own term; the first rung is not assumed to continue earning after it matures.

03

Put each bill after the maturity that is meant to fund it

The default also holds CAD 5,000 in a separate liquid reserve. It earns zero in this example. The household needs CAD 12,000 at each of five year-ends, after that year’s maturity proceeds arrive.

After the first release and bill, liquid cash is CAD 3,400. After year two it is CAD 2,216. It reaches its lowest year-end point at about CAD 1,163.23 in year four, then ends year five at about CAD 1,329.75.

The waterfall checks the endpoint: starting reserve plus returned principal plus interest, less CAD 60,000 of bills. The default reserve covers this particular annual calendar. It does not establish that a monthly living-expense schedule would remain funded between the shown dates.

04

Compare access timing even when the final proceeds are larger

The comparison puts the same CAD 50,000 into one five-year non-cashable term at the same rate. The starting reserve and five annual bills remain identical. This term releases no principal or interest before year five.

After the fourth annual bill, its unfunded cash position is negative CAD 43,000. The large fifth-year maturity cannot travel backward to meet those earlier commitments. The displayed additional starting cash measures that timing gap.

Because all capital compounds for five years in the single term, its final interest is larger under these assumptions. The chart therefore makes both facts visible: more late interest and less early access can occur together. No new borrowing, early redemption or additional cash injection is hidden in either path.

05

Treat renewal as a new cash-allocation decision

This is a run-off ladder: matured money remains cash or pays bills. Nothing automatically rolls into a new five-year term. A renewing ladder would need a different ledger, including the amount retained for spending and the amount locked away again.

The matrix changes annual needs and starting reserves while keeping the invested capital and rate selected. Its cells show extra starting cash needed at the deepest modeled shortfall, not simply the final deficit. Larger reserves belong outside the initial GIC purchases.

For a real plan, list the exact maturity dates, expected proceeds, account access conditions and spending deadlines. Review renewal instructions before each maturity. Taxes, deposit-insurance capacity and registered-account withdrawal rules are separate checks; none is inferred from this hypothetical cash schedule.
